stem: An adult develops acute fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and new confusion. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's priority response?

options.A: Suspect acute meningitis and escalate for emergency medical evaluation because this symptom cluster can occur with bacterial meningitis.
options.B: Rule out meningitis because all clients with bacterial meningitis must have a petechial rash.
options.C: Treat the symptoms as an uncomplicated tension headache because neck stiffness and confusion are expected with benign headache disorders.
options.D: Rule out bacterial meningitis if one component of the classic triad is absent because all classic findings must occur together.

rationale: A is correct. Current WHO and CDC guidance describes acute meningitis as potentially presenting with rapid-onset fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status. This constellation should trigger urgent evaluation because bacterial meningitis can progress rapidly and clinical findings alone do not identify the exact pathogen. B is incorrect because a petechial or purpuric rash is associated particularly with meningococcal disease and is not required for all bacterial meningitis. C dangerously normalizes meningeal and neurologic findings. D is incorrect because the classic findings are frequently incomplete; absence of one component does not reliably exclude bacterial meningitis.
educational_objective: Recognize acute fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status as a high-risk meningitis pattern requiring urgent evaluation while understanding that classic findings may be incomplete and no single absent sign reliably rules out bacterial meningitis.
source_organization: World Health Organization; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Library of Medicine / NCBI
source_document_title: WHO Guidelines on Meningitis Diagnosis, Treatment and Care — Introduction/Clinical Presentation; Meningococcal Disease Symptoms and Complications; Bacterial Meningitis — StatPearls
source_version_date: WHO meningitis guideline published 2025/current NCBI-hosted edition accessed 2026-08-17; CDC meningococcal symptoms page dated March 6, 2026; current StatPearls page accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: WHO guideline, section 1.5 Clinical presentation: acute meningitis is characterized by rapid onset of fever, neck stiffness, headache, photophobia and/or altered mental status; the classic combination should prompt strong suspicion, but all findings are not present in every case. CDC Meningococcal Disease Symptoms: fever, headache and stiff neck are common meningitis symptoms, often with confusion, nausea, photophobia or vomiting. NCBI StatPearls Bacterial Meningitis — History and Physical: fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status are the classic triad, but the complete triad is present in a minority of bacterial meningitis cases and absence of classic meningeal signs does not reliably rule disease out.
source_claim_supported: Acute meningitis can present with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and altered mental status; bacterial meningitis remains possible when the classic triad is incomplete, so a concerning symptom cluster requires urgent evaluation rather than rule-out from a missing single feature.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: recognize signs and symptoms of acute complications and intervene; apply pathophysiology and emergency-care knowledge to neurologic and infectious deterioration.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — recognition and escalation of suspected acute meningitis
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw list-recall question into an emergency recognition item. The final wording avoids teaching that every client displays a fixed 'classic' symptom set and explicitly guards against false rule-out from an incomplete triad or absent rash.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against the current WHO meningitis guideline, CDC's March 2026 meningococcal symptom guidance, and current NCBI Bacterial Meningitis review.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A uses a source-supported high-risk cluster without claiming pathogen confirmation. B wrongly makes rash mandatory. C cannot account for fever, meningismus and confusion. D falsely requires a complete triad.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; suspected meningitis requires urgent evaluation.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; rash is not required for bacterial meningitis.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; this is not a benign headache pattern.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; classic findings are often incomplete.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Viral and other meningitides can present similarly, so the answer says 'suspect acute meningitis' rather than diagnosing bacterial meningitis solely from symptoms. Among the choices, A is the only safe and evidence-concordant interpretation.
audit_findings.cueing: All options interpret the same neurologic/infectious presentation.
audit_findings.blueprint: Rapid recognition of a potentially fatal neurologic infection fits Physiological Adaptation.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked incomplete-triad prevalence, meningococcal rash specificity, and pathogen uncertainty. Removed any claim that the symptom cluster alone proves bacterial etiology and found no second defensible answer.
